transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2025-10-21
- Start: 16:00 PDT
- Duration: ~48 min
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Nina Patel (Orchid - Lead ML Eng), Carlos Ruiz (Orchid - Platform Eng), Elena Park (Orchid - Head Eng), Samir Das (Orchid - Security)

Summary:
Quick sandbox-style walkthrough of Redwood SDKs for Python and TypeScript, covering auth patterns (API keys, short-lived tokens), local env setup (.env and GH Actions), a brief demo of the Console quickstart, and an overview of Redwood Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization. Customer wanted to validate how fast they can get a POC running in their CI and what security knobs (KMS, SSO, VPC) are available.

Topics covered:
- Quickstart repo and examples (py + ts)
- API auth & environment variables (REDWOOD_API_KEY, roles, service tokens)
- Local dev vs CI (GitHub Actions secrets)
- Console walkthrough: model selection, route config, logs
- Redwood Optimize suggestions: batching, prefix caching, quantization profiles
- High level security: SOC 2, KMS/HSM, SSO/SAML, VPC/private deploy

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Liam, our solutions engineer. quick intro and then we'll jump into the sandbox.
[00:10] Nina: Hey all, Nina here. We're most interested in getting a PoC integrated into our CI and a sense of latency/cost tradeoffs.
[00:16] Carlos: Carlos — platform. We need to understand secrets and env management, also how to run small bench tests in our dev cluster.
[00:22] Liam: Awesome. We'll show the Python and TypeScript quickstarts, cover local env, GH Actions and then a Console tour to set routes, pick models, and look at metrics.
[00:35] Maya: Quick note — I'll drop the quickstart repo link in the zoom chat after this, and also the security docs.
[00:42] Samir: Great. Also SOC 2 and KMS questions later.
[00:45] Liam: Perfect. Ok jumping into the repo — first file is py_quickstart/README. For Python we install via pip install redwood-inference (note: transcription sometimes shows as 'redwood inference pip' in the README). We have a tiny sample that reads REDWOOD_API_KEY from env.
[01:05] Nina: Is the key a long-lived API key? we prefer short lived tokens for service accounts.
[01:09] Liam: By default you can use API keys for sandbox/dev. For production we recommend short-lived service tokens minted by your infra via our token service, or use the Private deployment with STS integration. Example: export REDWOOD_API_KEY="rk_live_..." for dev. We also show GH Actions example that pulls the secret from repo secrets as REDWOOD_API_KEY.
[01:32] Carlos: So GH Actions — do you have a sample workflow?
[01:35] Liam: Yes, there's .github/workflows/ci.yml. It runs pytest against a small smoke test that hits a local stub or the hosted Redwood endpoint depending on an env flag. We set REDWOOD_ENV="sandbox" or "prod".
[01:46] Maya: note: some customers call it Redwood Optimizer, we refer to it as Redwood Optimize in the docs — small naming mismatch in a couple of places.
[01:55] Elena: Can you show the TS example? our front-end team wants a typed client.
[02:00] Liam: Sure. In ts_quickstart we have a tiny example using @redwood/inference-client (again naming in repo is shorthand). import "{ RedwoodClient }" from "@redwood/inference-client"; const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY });
[02:18] Maya: important — when you ship to production we recommend per-route service accounts + RBAC, not a single org-wide key.
[02:25] Nina: What about KV cache? we saw a note about "KV cash" in an earlier doc, need clarification.
[02:29] Liam: ha, that's a transcription/artifact typo — it's KV cache. We support prefix caching and automatic KV caching to reduce repeated context costs.
[02:36] Carlos: For quantization and batching, can you give concrete defaults? our models are 4k context and typical prompt lengths 150 tokens.
[02:44] Liam: For that workload we'd suggest a Q4_0 or Q8_0 quant profile for dev trials, and enable batching with a max batch size of 8 and timeout of 20ms as a starting point. Redwood Optimize will analyze token distribution and suggest an optimal batch window — we can share the Optimize report from a sample run.
[03:05] Maya: also note that the runtime does kernel selection dynamically based on sequence length. so shorter inputs may route to a different optimized path.
[03:12] Samir: Security — do you support KMS integration and customer-managed keys?
[03:16] Liam: Yes, we support KMS/HSM integrations for Private deployments; hosted customers can use our managed keys but enterprise plans can bring-your-own KMS for encryption at rest. We also provide audit logs export, and SSO via SAML/Okta.
[03:30] Nina: What's the difference between hosted and Private (VPC) in terms of latency?
[03:34] Liam: Hosted is fastest to start and has multi-tenant nodes tuned for low latency. Private (VPC) gives you networking isolation and customer-managed keys but might add a few ms depending on your network egress. For strict data residency/regulatory needs we recommend Private.
[03:50] Carlos: Any notes on billing/credits for a POC?
[03:53] Maya: We'll offer trial credits for the POC. I'll include pricing ranges in the follow-up email.
[03:58] Liam: Ok demo time — I'm going to run the Python quickstart locally.
[04:02] [screen share starts]
[04:05] Liam: In the sample app run: python3 quickstart.py which calls client.generate("summarize", prompt). The script uses streaming and prints partial tokens; note our SDK supports both streaming and non-streaming.
[04:20] Liam: You might see some small transcription oddities in the doc where it calls "generate_chat" vs "generate" — both are supported depending on your client usage.
[04:32] Nina: How do we test latency from our cluster? do you have a small harness?
[04:36] Liam: We have a bench harness in examples/bench that uses locust or k6. It can be configured to run against the hosted endpoint or your Private endpoint. We'll share a pre-filled spreadsheet that captures P50/P95/P99, tokens/sec, and cost per 1k tokens.
[04:55] Carlos: Ok please share that spreadsheet.
[04:57] Maya: Will do. I'll attach the sheet and the sample harness link in the follow-up.
[05:02] Elena: Console question — can you walk through route config and the logs view?
[05:06] Liam: Yep. Switching to Console — go to Projects > Default Project > Routes. Here you can add a route, pin a model version (we show redwood-ggml-v2 as an example) and set fallback policies. The logs view shows per-request token breakdown and latency. You can also see token-level cost and per-token provider breakdown in some configurations.
[05:29] Carlos: Are there webhooks for usage or error alerts?
[05:31] Liam: Yes, you can push alerts to Slack or a webhook when errors exceed thresholds or latency spikes. We also have tracing hooks for distributed traces.
[05:40] Nina: For onboarding the front-end team, what's the cleanest pattern for client keys — do we put keys in the browser?
[05:44] Liam: No, never put secrets in the browser. Use a short-lived token minted by your backend or a server-side proxy. The TS client is intended for server/node use or edge runtimes where secrets are secured. For browser, use a mediated flow.
[05:58] Samir: Any compliance docs we can review quickly? SOC 2, ISO, penetration test reports?
[06:03] Maya: I'll attach the SOC 2 report summary and an infosec package. For Private customers we can arrange an NDA and deeper audit artifacts.
[06:12] Carlos: About RBAC — can we have per-team scopes?
[06:15] Liam: Yes, console supports roles and teams; you can create service accounts scoped to specific routes and grant read/write.
[06:22] Nina: Let's talk about the demo result — what would it take to show a PoC with our sample dataset in two weeks?
[06:28] Maya: If you can share a one-week sample and a list of success criteria (latency SLO, cost ceiling, quality metric) we can set up a trial environment and run baseline tests. Expect a first-pass report in ~5 business days after we get data.
[06:42] Elena: Timeline sounds good. We'll confirm internally.
[06:45] Liam: One more note on deployment: Dedicated capacity (reserved) is the path when you need predictable throughput; autoscaling policies can be configured with burst capacity for traffic surges.
[06:58] Nina: On the SDK side, do you support types for prompt templates?
[07:02] Liam: Yes, TS client exposes types and we have examples of prompt templating with typed inputs — we can add a small example for your schema.
[07:10] Maya: Ok wrapping up — recap of what we'll send: quickstart repo (py + ts), GH Actions example, bench harness + spreadsheet, security docs, and a proposal for a dedicated scoping call.
[07:22] Nina: Thanks, that would be great.
[07:25] Maya: I'll follow up with links and proposed times for the next call.
[07:30] Carlos: Thanks everyone.
[07:33] [meeting ends]

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-heard words (e.g., "KV cash"), and some library/package names abbreviated or inconsistent in the repo text.
